## Introduction

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs behave less like pathogens than like skin flora: acquired early, ubiquitous in healthy adults, and persisting as asymptomatic low-level infections [@antonsson2000; @doorbar2023]. At DNA level the reservoir is large and well mapped, with HPV in 61.3% of skin samples in shotgun metagenomics of healthy subjects [@ma2014] and beta-HPV in 92% of adults by skin swab [@rollison2019sites], across a diversity extending to 396 types, 229 of them previously unknown [@bzhalava2014]. What these figures cannot say is whether any of that material is transcribed.

The question matters because beta-HPV is a suspected cofactor in cSCC, particularly in organ-transplant recipients [@howley2015; @rollison2019]. Three accounts of its role are live and mutually compatible with the same data. Under "hit-and-run", beta-HPV acts early with ultraviolet radiation and is dispensable once the tumour is established [@viarisio2018; @dorfer2021]. Under the protective-immunity account, T-cell immunity to commensal papillomaviruses actively suppresses skin cancer, so viral loss reflects immune selection [@strickley2019]; that claim drew a formal exchange in the same journal [@lambert2021; @strickley2021], and has since been extended to show papillomavirus colonisation blocking mutant p53 clone expansion, with beta-HPV lost as those clones expand [@son2025]. A third account needs neither premise: the beta-HPV genome represses its own expression through E8\^E2, and immortalisation of keratinocytes requires that repressor to be inactivated [@rehm2022], so quiescence may simply be the viral default. All three predict declining viral activity from healthy skin to carcinoma, which is why measuring that decline more precisely cannot separate them.

Whether HPV is transcribed in cutaneous carcinoma has been asked directly, and the answers converge on no: in the original cSCC transcriptome study [@arron2011], in 12 skin lesions at a median 66 million reads [@hultin2019], in 345 post-transplant tumours at 35 million reads with transcription in 15 [@arroyomuhr2021], and in 23 risk-stratified biopsies with no expression against 64% DNA positivity [@vandiver2021]; E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization agrees, at 0.9% of 225 non-anogenital cutaneous SCC [@fujimoto2019]. The literature is not unanimous, since in situ hybridization demonstrated EV-HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 PCR-positive transplant cSCC [@purdie2005]. What no study has had is a denominator: these series run from 11 to 345 specimens, four of five are lesion-only with no unselected-skin comparator, the largest is confined to formalin-fixed transplant material, and none scores productive replication.

Public archives can supply that denominator, since the non-human reads discarded by standard pipelines carry the signal [@edgar2022], an approach already applied to skin [@leiendecker2023; @bhargava2025]. It is also booby-trapped: HeLa-derived HPV18 contaminates archived data extensively [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013], and depth and library chemistry both bound what any survey can detect. Here we re-mine public human RNA-seq across the skin spectrum, asking at what rate cutaneous HPV is transcribed, which types, and whether the infection is productive.
